question:
A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a car accident; he was extricated after 4 hours. He did not lose consciousness and does not have headache or nausea. He is in severe pain. He sustained severe injuries to both arms and the trauma team determines that surgical intervention is needed. Urinary catheterization shows dark colored urine. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. The patient is alert and oriented. Examination shows multiple injuries to the upper extremities, contusions on the trunk, and abdominal tenderness. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL
Leukocyte count 10,900/mm3
Platelet count 310,000/mm3
Serum
Na+ 137 mEq/L
K+ 6.8 mEq/L
Cl- 97 mEq/L
Glucose 168 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.7 mg/dL
Calcium 7.7 mg/dL
Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows a pH of 7.30 and a serum bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L. An ECG shows peaked T waves. A FAST scan of the abdomen is negative. Two large bore cannulas are inserted and intravenous fluids are administered. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Severe trauma" -> "Muscle injury" -> "Rhabdomyolysis" -> "Myoglobin release" -> "Dark urine" -> "Hyperkalemia" -> "ECG changes" -> "Intravenous calcium gluconate" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Severe trauma" -> "Muscle injury" -> "Rhabdomyolysis" -> "Myoglobin release" -> "Dark urine" -> "Hyperkalemia" -> "Metabolic acidosis" -> "Intravenous sodium bicarbonate" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Severe trauma" -> "Muscle injury" -> "Rhabdomyolysis" -> "Myoglobin release" -> "Dark urine" -> "Hyperkalemia" -> "ECG changes" -> "Intravenous insulin" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Severe trauma" -> "Blood loss" -> "Anemia" -> "Low hemoglobin" -> "Packed red blood cell transfusion" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Severe trauma" -> "Muscle injury" -> "Rhabdomyolysis" -> "Myoglobin release" -> "Dark urine" -> "Acute kidney injury" -> "Intravenous mannitol" -> 60%
analysis: The patient is likely experiencing rhabdomyolysis due to prolonged compression of muscles, as indicated by dark urine, elevated potassium, and acute kidney injury. The hyperkalemia is severe, as evidenced by the peaked T waves on ECG, and poses an immediate risk of cardiac arrhythmias. The most urgent step is to stabilize the cardiac membrane potential, which is achieved by administering intravenous calcium gluconate. This will help protect the heart while other measures to lower potassium levels are initiated.
